strengths: The paper addresses a very practical and important problem: sequentially monitoring the performance of a deployed model when labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant.

The proposed PPRM framework successfully integrates prediction-powered inference (PPI) with sequential risk monitoring (SRM) to yield anytime-valid confidence bounds with rigorous, assumption-free type-I error control.
The theoretical framework is comprehensive, including an adaptive procedure to optimize the reliance on unlabeled data (variance reduction) and a theoretical analysis of detection delay.

The empirical evaluation is exceptionally thorough, covering diverse domains such as image classification (CIFAR10-C), LLM QA monitoring (using LLM-as-a-judge), and wireless communications (channel equalization).
The appendix addresses realistic scenarios, such as intermittent labeling streams and non-monotonic shifts, proving the robustness and applicability of the method.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental, as the paper primarily combines two established frameworks: supervised risk monitoring (SRM) by Podkopaev & Ramdas (2022) and prediction-powered inference (PPI) by Angelopoulos et al. (2023).

To apply the time-uniform empirical Bernstein bound, the PPI estimates must be rescaled to [0,1], which requires setting a maximum parameter value \(\eta_{\max}\). The sensitivity of the bounds to the choice of \(\eta_{\max}\) is not thoroughly explored, which could affect the tightness of the bounds in practice.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical problem: monitoring the performance degradation of deployed machine learning models in dynamic environments where labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant.

The proposed PPRM framework elegantly combines sequential risk monitoring (SRM) with Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI), allowing the use of cheap synthetic labels from an auxiliary model while maintaining rigorous, assumption-free statistical guarantees on the type-I error rate.

The introduction of an online adaptive mechanism to optimize the reliance parameter (via variance reduction) is a valuable contribution that makes the method robust to the quality of the surrogate labeling model.

Excellent empirical evaluation across three highly diverse domains: image classification, large language model (LLM) QA, and telecommunications (channel equalization). The experimental results clearly show that PPRM achieves faster detection than SRM and URM while adhering to the false-alarm constraints.

The paper is very well-written, mathematically rigorous, and provides comprehensive analyses in the appendix, including an extension to the intermittent label stream setting and analytical approximations of the detection delay.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat incremental, as the work is largely a combination of two existing frameworks, namely SRM (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2022) and PPI/PPI++ (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a, b).

As analyzed in Proposition A.1, PPRM can suffer from a range-normalization penalty because the prediction-powered estimates expand the support of the loss. If the auxiliary predictor is poorly correlated with the true loss, PPRM can take longer to alarm than SRM. Although the adaptive mechanism effectively mitigates this, this fundamental limitation of PPI in a sequential setting should be discussed more prominently in the main text.

The method still requires a labeled calibration dataset from the nominal source distribution to establish the baseline risk upper bound, which might limit its applicability in scenarios where nominal labeled data is hard to acquire.

strengths: The paper is very well-written, clearly presented, and the motivation for sequential risk monitoring under label scarcity is strong.
The proposed PPRM framework successfully provides anytime-valid, assumption-free type-I error guarantees by leveraging prediction-powered inference (PPI).
The online adaptive procedure for adjusting the hyperparameter \(\eta_t\) is practical and theoretically grounded in minimizing the variance of the estimator.
The evaluation is diverse, spanning image classification, LLM question-answering, and a wireless channel equalization task.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty of the paper is quite limited. The work is a relatively straightforward combination of Supervised Risk Monitoring (SRM) (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2022) and Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI/PPI++) (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a; 2023b). The key estimators, concentration bounds, and hyperparameter optimization formulas are directly adopted from these prior works.

The assumption that a stream of true labeled data is available synchronously (with \(n_t \ge 1\) at every single time step \(t\)) is highly optimistic for real-world monitoring applications where label acquisition is typically slow, delayed, or batch-processed. If real-time labels are readily available at every step, the practical necessity of semi-supervised estimation is partially diminished.

The benefit of the method (reducing the time to alarm) relies heavily on the quality of the predictive model \(f_p\). However, under severe, unseen distribution shifts, the predictive model \(f_p\) itself is likely to experience performance degradation, which reduces the covariance between the surrogate and true risks and may cause PPRM to revert to the performance of SRM.

The comparison with Unsupervised Risk Monitoring (URM) is somewhat unfair because URM operates under a zero-test-label constraint, whereas PPRM uses test-time labels. A more rigorous baseline comparison would involve other sequential testing or change-point detection methods operating under the same budget of labeled data.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly practical and important problem: continuously monitoring the performance of deployed machine learning models when labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is abundant.

By leveraging prediction-powered inference (PPI), the proposed PPRM method maintains rigorous, distribution-free, and finite-sample guarantees on the false alarm rate without requiring assumptions on the accuracy of the surrogate label generator.

The introduction of an online, adaptive hyperparameter optimization strategy (minimizing the one-step variance of the estimator using a sliding window) is sound and shown to improve detection latency.

The experimental evaluation is diverse and extensive, spanning classic image classification (CIFAR-10-C), large language models (evaluating Qwen2-VL with LLM-as-a-judge), and wireless communication (channel equalization).
weaknesses: The core components of the theoretical framework are largely combinations of existing tools: the sequential testing relies on Howard et al.'s conjugate-mixture empirical Bernstein bounds, and the risk estimation leverages PPI/PPI++ directly.

PPRM assumes a strictly positive number of labeled samples ($n_t \geq 1$) at each monitoring step. In extremely high-throughput or highly resource-constrained edge environments, obtaining even one ground-truth label per step can be challenging, which limits applicability compared to purely unsupervised methods.

The paper lacks a detailed sensitivity analysis regarding the sliding window size $L$ used to estimate the adaptive parameter $\eta_t$. It is unclear how robust the method is to suboptimal choices of $L$ under highly non-stationary environments.

strengths: Highly relevant and practical problem setting: addressing the monitoring of deployed machine learning models under severe labeling constraints by utilizing semi-supervised data streams.

Solid theoretical foundation: the proposed PPRM framework inherits the assumption-free, finite-sample guarantees on the probability of false alarm (PFA) from supervised risk monitoring (SRM) while effectively boosting power.
Adaptive variance reduction: the paper derives an optimal parameter selection strategy for the reliance on unlabeled data (\eta_t) and provides a practical online plug-in estimator.

Comprehensive and diverse experimental validation: evaluations span multiple domains, including image classification (CIFAR-10-C), LLM question-answering evaluation, and physical-layer telecommunication tasks (channel equalization).
weaknesses: The methodological contribution is somewhat incremental, as it primarily combines existing components from supervised sequential risk monitoring (Podkopaev & Ramdas, 2021) and prediction-powered inference (Angelopoulos et al., 2023a; 2023b).
The requirement of having at least one labeled sample ($n_t \ge 1$) at every discrete monitoring time step can be a strong assumption in highly latent labeling environments.
The paper lacks a sensitivity analysis regarding the choice of the sliding window size $L$ used for the online estimation of the adaptive hyperparameter $\eta_t$.

strengths: Strong Motivation & Practical Relevance: The paper addresses a highly practical and realistic setting in machine learning deployment: monitoring running risk sequentially under limited availability of labeled data.

Solid Theoretical Foundation: By leveraging Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI), the proposed PPRM method guarantees anytime-valid false alarm control without imposing any assumptions on the quality of the surrogate labeling model.

Adaptive Reliance on Unlabeled Data: The derivation and sequential estimation of the optimal weight parameter dynamically adjusts the reliance on unlabeled data, leading to tighter risk lower bounds and faster detection of harmful shifts.
Diverse and Thorough Evaluation: The method is evaluated across three distinct and modern domains: image classification (CIFAR-10-C), LLM QA monitoring, and wireless telecommunications.
weaknesses: Incremental Technical Novelty: The paper is primarily a clever combination of existing tools: Supervised Risk Monitoring (SRM) from Podkopaev & Ramdas (2021), PPI++ from Angelopoulos et al. (2023b), and sequential concentration bounds from Howard et al. (2021).

Assumption of Synchronous Labeled Data: The framework requires a strictly positive number of labeled samples (at least 1) at each discrete monitoring step. In real-world stream processing, labeled feedback is often delayed or asynchronous, and the impact of delayed labels on anytime-validity is not thoroughly discussed.

Sensitivity of Sliding Window for Parameter Tuning: The estimation of the optimal weight relies on a sliding window of size L. Under rapid or non-monotonic distribution shifts, a fixed window size might lead to outdated estimates, potentially hurting detection power. A discussion or sensitivity analysis regarding the window size L is missing.
